package_info.why_malicious: These packages contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely (RCE) by exploiting unsafe string interpolation (log4j, commons-text) or unsafe class loader/module access (spring-framework). Attackers can inject malicious payloads through crafted input, leading to system compromise, data exfiltration, or further lateral movement.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when user input is logged or interpolated in log messages)
execution_context.file_location: log4j core logging logic (e.g., PatternLayout, message formatting in log4j-core JAR)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Performs a JNDI lookup using an attacker-controlled LDAP URL embedded in a log message. If the LDAP server responds with a malicious Java class, log4j loads and executes it, resulting in remote code execution on the server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allows untrusted input in log messages to trigger network lookups and load remote code via JNDI, enabling attackers to execute arbitrary code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging libraries are expected to record messages, not execute code or perform network lookups based on log content. Accepting untrusted input for JNDI lookups violates this principle.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimate in enterprise Java for resource discovery, but not in log message formatting where user input is involved.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages
Network requests initiated during log message processing
Dynamic loading of Java classes from remote LDAP servers
Use of log4j-core versions prior to 2.17.1

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when variable interpolation is performed on user-controlled input)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Performs variable interpolation using attacker-controlled prefix and name. If a malicious or unsafe Lookup implementation is available, this can trigger network lookups or code execution, potentially leading to RCE.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allows attacker-controlled input to specify lookup prefixes, enabling arbitrary lookups (including network or script execution) if unsafe lookups are enabled.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: String interpolation should only resolve safe, local variables. Allowing user input to control lookup mechanisms introduces the risk of code execution or network access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Variable interpolation is common for configuration, but should be restricted to predefined, safe values and not allow arbitrary lookup prefixes from user input.
key_indicators: Unrestricted use of ${...} patterns in user-controlled input
Ability to specify custom lookup prefixes (e.g., 'script', 'url', 'dns', 'jndi')
Network or code execution side effects during string interpolation
Use of commons-text versions prior to 1.10.0

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when application is deployed as WAR on Tomcat, JDK 9+ and data binding occurs via web requests)
execution_context.file_location: Spring Framework data binding logic (e.g., spring-beans, spring-webmvc in spring-framework JARs)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Allows access to the class's module and class loader through data binding. In vulnerable Spring Framework versions, this can be exploited to manipulate the class loader and achieve remote code execution via crafted web requests.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exposes internal class loader and module access via data binding, which can be exploited by attackers to load arbitrary classes or resources, leading to RCE.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Frameworks should not expose sensitive internals like class loader or module access through user-controllable properties in web requests.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Reflection and module access are legitimate in advanced Java programming, but not when exposed to user input via web request data binding.
key_indicators: Exposure of getModule() or class loader access via data binding
Ability to manipulate class loader or module from user input
RCE via crafted web requests in specific deployment scenarios (WAR on Tomcat, JDK 9+)
Use of vulnerable spring-framework versions (5.3.0-5.3.17, 5.2.0-5.2.19, older)

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends crafted input (such as a log message, web request, or interpolated string) containing a malicious payload designed to exploit the vulnerable library.
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggering of vulnerable code paths in the affected library, processing the malicious input.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable library processes the input, performing unsafe interpolation (log4j, commons-text) or exposing class loader/module access (spring-framework) as dictated by attacker input.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of network requests, loading of remote code, or manipulation of class loader, depending on the exploit path.

attack_chain.action: Remote code execution is achieved, allowing the attacker to run arbitrary code on the server, potentially gaining full control.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data exfiltration, installation of malware, or further lateral movement within the environment.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected outbound network requests (e.g., LDAP, RMI, HTTP) during log message processing or string interpolation
Presence of ${jndi:...} or similar variable patterns in log messages or user input fields
Exposure of class loader or module access (e.g., getModule()) via web request data binding in Spring applications
Dynamic loading of Java classes from remote servers during normal application operation
file_indicators: Presence of vulnerable spring-beans or spring-webmvc JARs (versions 5.3.0-5.3.17, 5.2.0-5.2.19, or older)
Application packaged as WAR and deployed on Tomcat (for Spring4Shell scenarios)
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP requests to untrusted or unexpected domains during log processing or string interpolation
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., domains specified in ${jndi:ldap://...}) triggered by application input
Unusual DNS lookups or network activity correlated with log or string processing events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for use of vulnerable library versions by scanning application dependencies. Inspect logs and user input for suspicious patterns such as ${jndi:...} or custom lookup prefixes in string interpolation. Alert on unexpected outbound network requests (LDAP, RMI, HTTP) from application servers during log or string processing. Use static analysis to detect exposure of class loader or module access via data binding in Spring applications. Upgrade all affected libraries to patched versions to mitigate risk.
